Missouri Republicans learned this month what happens when a party trades its principles for a personality. Ann Wagner represented the 2nd Congressional District since 2013. She entered the summer with roughly $4.2 million in the bank against her opponent’s $242,000.
She lost by nearly five percentage points to Fred Wellman, who will be the first Democrat to hold the seat since the early 1990s. In Jefferson City, Democrats broke the Republican supermajorities in both the House and the Senate.
There will be excuses about a “national blue wave” or a court ruling that kept the 2022 district lines in place. Both mattered, but neither fully explains what went wrong. The blue wave was built on millions of individual votes and verdicts, and Republicans should pay attention to the concerns behind them: what groceries cost, what gas costs, and whether Washington is making their lives more secure or less.
The good news is that the Republican Party already has answers.
They are our own. Our Republican Legacy, co-founded by former Missouri Sen. John Danforth, rests on five principles: the Constitution, unity, fiscal responsibility, free enterprise and peace through strength. Three of them speak directly to the concerns voters expressed at the ballot box.
Start with free enterprise. Soybeans are Missouri’s most valuable crop, worth roughly $2.9 billion in 2025. China, once the largest buyer, sharply curtailed purchases of American soybeans during the trade war. Even after a deal, its tariff on our soybeans stood at 13 percent at the start of this year, versus 3 percent on beans from Brazil and Argentina. Washington picked a fight, and Missouri farmers got the bill.
Tariffs are taxes, and Americans bear the costs. When the government imposes tariffs that hurt farmers and then writes them relief checks, that is not conservatism. It is the crony capitalism Republicans once spent careers opposing, with political favors picking winners and losers instead of markets.
The same goes for peace through strength. Reagan’s phrase never meant reaching for force first, and it never meant walking away from friends. It meant being strong and reliable enough that adversaries think twice and allies sleep well.
Today, our allies, from Kyiv to Seoul, have reason to wonder whether America’s word still holds. Whatever one thinks of the war with Iran, Missourians are paying for it at the pump, and Wagner’s challenger made her support for it a campaign issue.
Peace through strength is the opposite of drift and bluster: steady alliances, credible deterrence and the patience to keep wars from starting in the first place.
Then there is unity, and Missouri voters sent a message Republicans should heed. Wellman held 13 town halls, campaigned in every corner of the district and talked about restoring faith in government rather than demonizing the other side.
In St. Charles County, where Wagner won by about 16,000 votes in 2024, her margin shrank to roughly 4,000. That shift should force Republicans to consider whether voters are growing tired of politics built on division. Even Wagner’s concession pointed the way: she called Wellman late Tuesday night, and he described her as gracious. Unity used to be something Republicans did better than anyone. It can be again.

Nowhere in any running rulebook does it say you have to train for a 5K or 10K before signing up for a half marathon. As a beginner, 13.1 miles is an awesome way to approach long-distance running. You just need a plan that meets you where you’re at right now and progresses gradually to get you to the starting line feeling strong.
Cut to Runner’s World’s 20-week beginner half marathon plan created by Meg Takacs, C.P.T., a UESCA-certified running coach and founder of the Movement and Miles app.
It balances three key workouts designed to help you build endurance safely, recover well, and get comfortable with longer distances. You’ll spread these workouts throughout 20 weeks, which gives you plenty of time to build rather than your typical 10- or 14-week plan.
Each workout progresses as you move through the plan, so it’s a good idea to familiarize yourself with their basic structure and purpose before you jump into training. Here’s how to get the most out of each workout.
DOWNLOAD YOUR ZERO TO HALF PLAN HERE
3 Key Workouts to Go From Zero to Your First Half Marathon
Run/Walk
Run/walks help you build aerobic fitness and endurance gradually. You’ll start with a one-minute run followed by a one-minute walk for 20 minutes total, adding one minute to the run interval every session. With run/walks starting at three times a week, you’ll work up to a 10-mile run/walk in week 16, where you run for 20-minute intervals and walk for two minutes (this is your weekend long run).
Do the run intervals at a comfortable, low-intensity pace, meaning you should be able to hold a conversation with a friend the whole time. On a scale of 1 to 10 for rate of perceived exertion (RPE), aim for a 2 to 4 for effort level, with 1 being easy like a walk and 10 meaning all-out effort.
Continuous Easy Run
In week four of this plan, you’ll start incorporating continuous easy runs, beginning with 25 minutes at a truly easy effort. The longest continuous run you will complete is 8 miles with as few walk breaks as possible by week 17.
Throughout the plan, there’s more of a focus on time-based easy runs rather than distance. “For beginners, time on your feet is more important than mileage in order to get your body gradually acclimated to running,” Takacs previously told Runner’s World.
Speed Workout
The first of your weekly speed workouts begins in week 3. You’ll complete 400-meter repeats at a moderate effort with two-minute walks in between. Moderate effort is slightly above your easy effort, reaching a 4 to 6 out of 10 RPE. “The goal is to try and run each repeat faster than the last,” Takacs adds.
You should still be able to speak during the work intervals, but you’re breathing heavier and can only talk in phrases. Over the course of the training plan, you’ll work your way up to longer intervals, like 800-meter, 1200-meter, and mile repeats.
3 Tips for Making the Most of Your First Half-Marathon Training Cycle
Add in Strides
Short postrun strides help build speed and leg turnover, and you’ll find them sprinkled throughout your plan. These accelerations will help you build more speed, improve your running form by getting your legs to turn over quicker, and boost your confidence.
The goal of strides is to run at a hard effort for 10 to 15 seconds, but it doesn’t have to be an all-out sprint. Aim for a 7 to 10 RPE; you should only be able to say a word or three at a time.

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A $105 Billion to $11 Billion AI Revenue Gap
America’s two leading AI labs now bring in $105 billion a year in annualized revenue. China’s six top AI companies bring in about $11 billion combined. That estimate comes from Epoch AI’s 2026 comparison of run rates. It credits Anthropic with approximately $65 billion and OpenAI with $40 billion. On the other side are ByteDance, Alibaba (NYSE:BABA | BABA Price Prediction), Z.ai, Moonshot AI, DeepSeek, and MiniMax.
The U.S. pair generated about 9.5 times the Chinese group’s run rate, a gap of approximately $94 billion. Anthropic alone generated nearly six times the Chinese total. That gap arrives days before Anthropic’s IPO on Nov. 19, which carries a proposed valuation of $1.4 trillion.
What the Gap Means for Anthropic’s Valuation
The comparison already downplays Anthropic’s lead. The company’s IPO disclosures put annualized revenue at approximately $81 billion by October. Drawn from different reporting periods, the estimates cover only these companies and leave out much of the AI revenue earned in each country.
Even with that catch, the gap shows how much further ahead U.S. labs are at selling AI. Enterprises are paying for American frontier models at scale, and the distribution channels are expanding. On the third-quarter call for Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), CEO Andy Jassy said Bedrock token volume is growing nearly 17x year-over-year[1], and Fortune 500 companies are spending nearly 7x more on the service. He tied that demand directly to the labs: “We have both closed models and models like Anthropic and OpenAI’s models.”[1] AWS backlog stands at $578 billion.
China’s leaders are growing, but from a smaller base. Alibaba’s AI cloud and compute revenue rose 45% YoY[2], and Omdia ranks it first in China’s AI cloud market with a 38.1% share. The capital behind each side shows the same imbalance. Alibaba spent $9.97 billion[2] on capex in its latest quarter. Amazon spent $77.26 billion[3] in its quarter and repeated full-year 2026 cash capex of approximately $220 billion for AI infrastructure.
Why Anthropic’s Revenue Lead Could Keep Widening
Anthropic heads to market with the largest revenue base in this comparison, and that base kept growing after the Epoch AI figures were compiled. The jump from $65 billion to $81 billion by October shows that its sales are compounding.
The infrastructure behind U.S. AI is scaling to match. Jassy said Amazon has “very good visibility into 2027 and 2028 and some of 2029 too”[1] on large customer capacity commitments. Alphabet‘s (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google Cloud revenue rose 103% YoY[4] to $30.71 billion. Both point to broad demand from paying customers, and the expansion behind that demand (power, cooling, networking) is where a lot of the next wave of AI winners will come from (we covered seven of those suppliers in a free report). Chinese rivals, meanwhile, work under export controls that Anthropic’s own filing lists among its regulatory risk factors, and recent chip-access concerns have pushed down Chinese AI stocks.

AMD Just Beat Nvidia by the Widest Margin Since 1999
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
In the five trading days through Thursday, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD | AMD Price Prediction) rose 44.7%, from $404.40 to $585.30. Over the same period, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell 8.5%, from $181.60 to $166.19.
By our calculation, that 53.2-percentage-point gap is the widest five-day spread in AMD’s favor across 6,997 trading days, which covers all 27 years since Nvidia’s January 1999 IPO. AMD had record results and new customer orders, while Nvidia lost its chief executive.
AMD’s Spread Broke a Record Set in 2016
The old high was 50.1 points in the five days to April 22, 2016, when AMD rose 47.8%, and Nvidia fell 2.3%. Nvidia’s fall this time was much steeper than in 2016, so it accounts for more of the gap.
From Friday to Friday, AMD gained 18.93% from $449.04, and Nvidia lost 12.75% from $186.64. By our calculation, that 31.7-point gap is still the widest since the five days to October 10, 2025.
Record Revenue and Cloud Wins Power AMD
AMD jumped 11.04% on November 6 after third-quarter revenue reached a record $13.4 billion, up 45%. Data center revenue rose about 97%, so the business that competes head-on with Nvidia powered the quarter.
On November 11, AMD added 7.32% to $552.90. That move followed results from CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), a spot on a preferred chip list from Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS), and a cloud deal with Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL) unit Google for fifth-generation EPYC chips. CEO Lisa Su said “demand is higher than supply”[1] and guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion[2] as Helios racks and Venice processors ramp.
Nvidia Lost Its CEO and a Sixth Straight Week
On November 12, Nvidia said Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO, and director and named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. The stock then posted its sixth straight weekly loss.
The market usually absorbs reported results within days, but uncertainty over who leads a company lasts until the board names a permanent replacement. Size also helps explain the gap, because AMD’s $875.9 billion market value takes far less new money to move sharply than Nvidia’s $3.93 trillion. Nvidia still controls its CUDA software platform and reported $96.22 billion in revenue last quarter, so a credible CEO pick could steady the stock.
On Friday, AMD fell 8.75% to $534.06, while Nvidia slipped 2.01% to $162.85. In after-hours trading, AMD changed hands at $521.24 and Nvidia at $161.04.
A one-day drop that steep after a 44.7% run suggests that many late buyers were chasing momentum. AMD is also still about 19% below its 52-week high of $658.52.
AMD’s Growth Outlook Faces a Valuation Test
AMD has the stronger near-term growth case. Management expects 2027 revenue to grow more than 80%[1], with data center making up more than 80% of sales.
The stock swings hard in both directions, and a trailing P/E of 202 leaves little room for a guidance miss. Nvidia’s lower price could draw renewed interest once it names a permanent CEO. Until then, AMD has the clearer growth story, and its reported numbers support it.

The last few months haven't been the best for Bank of America [NYSE: BAC].
Trouble for the nation's second-largest bank went mainstream this October when the U.S. Department of the Treasury alleged Bank of America (BofA) put its revenues over safety regulations with weak anti-money laundering and sanctions practices. The combined penalties levied against the bank from the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Office of Foreign Assets Control totaled $1.21 billion.

According to FinCEN, BofA failed to report $5 billion in "suspicious transactions," some allegedly related to "chinese money laundering networks" and "illicit finance along the southwest border," including cartels.
At the time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent championed these penalties, claiming, "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."
Moneywise reached out to Bank of America for further comment. In response, a BofA spokesperson said, "Financial crime compliance is serious and we are responsible for getting it right. We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 OCC Consent Order and FinCEN's investigation.
"We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."
Senator Warren wants a Capitol Hill grilling
Despite being the third-largest penalty ever levied by the Treasury, some lawmakers balked at the number, claiming $1.21 billion was not severe enough. Senator Elizabeth Warren, who pushed for a criminal investigation, was chief among them.
After the news broke, Warren took to X and called the payment a "slap on the wrist." Rather than settling for these civil penalties, Warren wants BofA's executives to face the music on Capitol Hill.
As she wrote on X, "CEO Brian Moynihan owes Congress answers, and we need a criminal investigation into the apparent violation of our anti-money-laundering laws. I've long said big bank CEOs should be held personally accountable if their banks break the law."
Despite Warren's petition to the Department of Justice, there's no official word on a criminal investigation into Bank of America. However, a new securities class action lawsuit from the law firm Hagens Berman is hanging over Bank of America. For BofA shareholders, Hagens Berman's litigation might offer a slight financial reprieve.
Understandably, Bank of America's stock hasn't been so hot following the Treasury's allegations. Shares in this bank slumped 4.5% after news of the $1.21 billion penalty broke. At the time of writing, BofA shareholders are down about 7.8% year to date. By comparison, the S&P 500 is up about 10.3% in 2026.
But even if your BofA shares are down, you may still get some cash back thanks to Hagens Berman's lawsuit. Anyone who held BofA stock between August 1, 2025, and October 13, 2026, on a U.S. exchange and experienced "substantial losses" could file a claim to potentially recover damages.

PEORIA, Ariz. -- In some Arizona Fall League seasons, there's a player who has that it factor. Ronald Acuña Jr. Vladimir Guerrero Jr. Kevin McGonigle.
This year, it's Cardinals outfielder Tai Peete. Not only was he the developmental circuit's most electric player, he also was its Offensive Player of the Year. He slashed .351/.441/.662, set an AFL record by tripling in four consecutive games, topped the circuit with 20 steals and ranked in the top five in nine offensive categories. He also finished second in the Home Run Derby on Fall Stars Game weekend.

"Tai does it all," said Peoria Javelinas teammate Ike Irish (Orioles), who hits with Peete during the offseason. "He can steal, he can run, he can throw, he can bang. He's the real deal and he puts the work in. He grinds in the cages. He's perfecting his swing every day. So I'm not really shocked by this."
Peete's virtuoso performance in the Fall League caps an eventful year. A supplemental first-round pick by the Mariners in 2023, he switched organizations this February in a trade for Brendan Donovan. After never having to deal with any sort of serious injury, he sustained a concussion when he was tagged in the head in late May and then came down with an illness that sapped him of 25 pounds, sidelining him for six weeks.
When he returned, Peete -- the Cardinals' No. 17 prospect -- played the best ball of his career. He batted .339/.386/.614 with 10 homers and 11 steals in 39 games between High-A and Double-A, then tore up the Fall League.
Built like a wide receiver at 6-foot-2 and 193 pounds, Peete also features the well above-average speed befitting the position. He has exceptional bat speed, plus raw power and a strong arm that delivered fastballs up to 96 mph when he pitched at Trinity Christian HS in Sharpsburg, Ga. Age is also on his side, as he just turned 21 in August.
There never has been any question about Peete's tools and upside, but there have been some concerns about his bat. He hit .217 last year in High-A and carried a career 31 percent strikeout rate before he was sidelined in the middle of this season.
Peete cut his K rate to 23 percent in the final two months of Minor League play and 18 percent in the AFL. If he can make that kind of contact, he'll be a star.
Peete's swing-and-miss issues stem in large part from an extremely aggressive approach. Interestingly, he has fished for more pitches out of the zone than usual during his hot streak. His chase rate was 35 percent from July through September and 33 percent in Arizona, compared to 28 percent in his first three-plus seasons as a pro.

Key Takeaways
- Ilex Capital Partners, a fund with $5.15 billion of US stocks, sold its whole stakes in Keurig Dr Pepper, Yum! Brands and Philip Morris International in the third quarter, its 13F shows.
- Each stake was about 3% of the fund at June 30. Keurig Dr Pepper and Philip Morris have each risen 10% or more since Sept. 30.
- For all three stocks, Wall Street’s average price targets are only 5% to 9% above the latest close.
- Keurig Dr Pepper has the best case of the three: adjusted EPS rose 22.2% last quarter, and the stock trades at 15x forward earnings.
A $5.2 billion fund just walked away from three of the best-known names in consumer stocks: Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP), Yum! Brands (YUM) and Philip Morris International (PM).
Ilex Capital Partners (UK) held all three at June 30 and none at Sept. 30, according to its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13. The filing lists $5.15 billion of US stocks across 252 positions. Each of the three was about 3% of the portfolio a quarter earlier. A 13F doesn’t say when in the quarter a fund sold, or why.
Keurig Dr Pepper kept delivering
Ilex’s 4.97 million Keurig Dr Pepper shares were worth $163 million at June 30, 3.3% of the fund. The stock is up 11% since Sept. 30, and the third quarter gave investors plenty to like. Leaving out JDE Peet’s, which Keurig Dr Pepper bought on April 1, net sales rose 8.6%. Adjusted EPS jumped 22.2% to $0.66, the company said in its Nov. 3 release, and management reaffirmed its full-year guidance.
Analysts have been raising their targets since the spring:
The average target from 19 analysts has climbed from a low of $33 in April to $38, just 5% above the latest close. At 15x forward earnings, that’s still a modest price for a business growing like this.
TIKR tracks 19 analysts on Keurig Dr Pepper. How many say “Buy”?
See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Keurig Dr Pepper, along with Wall Street’s revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Keurig Dr Pepper’s Analyst Ratings
Yum! Brands needs Taco Bell back on track
Yum! Brands hasn’t had the same run. Ilex held 1.02 million shares at June 30, worth $162 million and 3.3% of the fund. The stock is up just 0.9% since Sept. 30. Ilex didn’t give up on restaurants, though: at Sept. 30 it held 50% more Chipotle Mexican Grill shares than three months earlier, which made Chipotle the fund’s No. 4 holding.
Taco Bell is Yum’s problem. Its U.S. same-store sales fell 4% in the third quarter, after a 7% gain a year earlier. CEO Chris Turner said Taco Bell’s U.S. same-store sales have beaten the rest of the quick-service industry since the end of September. Yum’s fourth-quarter report, due early next year, will show whether that held up.
Analysts have been more upbeat than the stock:
The average target from 25 analysts rose from $165 a year ago to $175, 9% above the latest close. But at 25x forward earnings, investors are already paying for a recovery Taco Bell hasn’t delivered yet.
Philip Morris has already had its run
Philip Morris International is the other sale that kept climbing, up 10% since Sept. 30. Ilex held 804,943 shares at June 30, worth $146 million and 3.0% of the fund.

Coca-Cola and J&J Just Hit Record Highs. A 62-Year-Old Put $300,000 Into Them and Procter & Gamble in 2016. Here’s How Much the Now 72-Year-Old Gets Paid Every Single Month
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
On Monday, Nov. 14, 2016, the first trading day after the election week, a 62-year-old put $300,000 into three companies whose products he had used every day of his life: Johnson & Johnson (J&J), Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola, $100,000 in each. Call him Walt. He had just sold a rental duplex, he was still two years from claiming Social Security, and he wanted checks he could count on. The 10-year Treasury paid 2.23% that Monday. The three stocks paid more, and they had raised their payouts every year for half a century.
Ten years later, to the day, Walt is 72. His shares have never been touched, and the three companies have kept raising the dividend every year: Johnson & Johnson for 64 straight years, Coca-Cola for 64, Procter & Gamble for 70. The checks now add up to $14,983 a year, which is $1,249 a month, call it $1,250. He has cashed $121,100 of dividends along the way, and the $300,000 of stock is worth about $690,300 after Coca-Cola and Johnson & Johnson both closed at record highs on Friday.
Walt is a scenario. The prices, the dividend history and the tax rules are real, pulled from Alpha Vantage’s daily record of each stock and from the IRS tables for 2026. Ten years of raises from household names read as proof that a retiree can out-earn a bond without taking a trader’s risk. The limit sits in the same numbers: a buyer at Friday’s prices gets about 2.2%, less than half of what Walt earns on his cost, and three stocks is a thin basket for anyone’s income.
What $300,000 bought in 2016
At the Nov. 14, 2016 closes, $100,000 bought whole shares only:
Johnson & Johnson closed at $116.60. That bought 857 shares for $99,926.20. The quarterly dividend was $0.80, so the shares yielded 2.74%.
Procter & Gamble closed at $83.00. That bought 1,204 shares for $99,932.00. The quarterly dividend was $0.6695, a 3.23% yield.
Coca-Cola closed at $41.17. That bought 2,428 shares for $99,960.76. The quarterly dividend was $0.35, a 3.40% yield.
Total spent: $299,818.96, with $181.04 left in cash. At those first rates the three positions paid $9,365.91 a year, about $780 a month. Every one of the 120 dividends since then has been paid, 40 from each company, and not one was smaller than the one before it.
The checks today
Each company raised again in 2026. Johnson & Johnson lifted its quarterly dividend 3.1% in April to $1.34, its 64th straight annual increase. Procter & Gamble raised 3% in April to $1.0885, its 70th. Coca-Cola raised about 4% in February to $0.53, its 64th. On Walt’s share counts:
Johnson & Johnson: 857 shares at $5.36 a year pay $4,593.52, or $1,148.38 a quarter.
Procter & Gamble: 1,204 shares at $4.354 a year pay $5,242.22, or $1,310.55 a quarter.
Coca-Cola: 2,428 shares at $2.12 a year pay $5,147.36, or $1,286.84 a quarter.
Together that is $14,983.10 a year, $1,248.59 a month on average. The checks do not arrive on the first of every month. Procter & Gamble pays in February, May, August and November; Johnson & Johnson in March, June, September and December; Coca-Cola in April, July, October and December. He Thinks His $200,000 S&P 500 401(k) Spreads His AI Risk. Two Alphabet Share Classes Put $10,380 in One Company. A 20% Drop Could Cost Him $2,076
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Consider a hypothetical 58-year-old with $200,000 of his 401(k) in an S&P 500 index fund. He figures every company is a thin piece of his savings and that no single AI stock can do much damage. The October 22 holdings that State Street published for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) show something he missed: Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction) is listed twice.
Why Alphabet Holds Two Seats in Your Index Fund
Alphabet has two share classes that trade publicly. Class A shares (GOOGL) carry voting rights. Alphabet Class C (NASDAQ:GOOG) has none. Class B is held by insiders and does not trade publicly. The S&P 500 weights stocks by market value, and it gives each public class its own position.
The October 22 report put Class A at 2.88% of the fund and Class C at 2.31%. Together, that’s 5.19% riding on one management team, one balance sheet and one capital spending plan.
This was already true earlier in the year. SPY’s March fact sheet listed the two classes at 3% and 2%. Because the classes appear on separate lines of a holdings screen, the combined stake is easy to miss.
A 20% Drop in One Stock Takes $2,076 From His Account
At a combined 5.19% weight, $10,380 of his $200,000 is tied to Alphabet.
Say both share classes fall 20% and every other holding stays flat. His account would lose about $2,076, or roughly 1% of his balance, because of one company.
Alphabet has already come close to that kind of drop. Its Class A shares fell from about $353 on October 12 to $299 on November 12, a slide of roughly 15% in one month. The stock’s 52-week high was nearly $409.
An equal-weight fund produces a very different number. In the July 31 filing for the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSEARCA:RSP), the two Alphabet classes together made up about 0.19% of assets.
On $200,000, that works out to roughly $388, about 27 times smaller than his current exposure.
Alphabet’s AI Spending Now Affects His Retirement Balance
Alphabet’s third-quarter results show why this exposure carries more risk than it used to. Google Cloud revenue grew 103% to $31 billion.
Capital spending for the quarter reached $51 billion, up 114%, which left free cash flow at negative $9 billion.
Management credits the spending for the growth. CEO Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud revenue jumped 103% as demand for AI infrastructure surged. Still, Alphabet missed Wall Street’s revenue estimates. Earnings came to $2.12 a share, weighed down by an $8.7 billion loss on equity investments.
Alphabet is hardly alone. Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that U.S. hyperscalers will spend roughly $857 billion on capital projects in 2026. Alphabet’s links to AI valuations also go beyond its own data centers: Reuters reports that Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Google stand to gain a large windfall from an Anthropic IPO. The AI build-out may well pay off. The issue for a saver near retirement is position size. At 58, a sharp drop just before withdrawals begin does more damage than the same drop at 35.
Three Moves to Make Before Your Next Rebalance
- Add every share class together. Pull the holdings for each fund in your 401(k), IRAs and brokerage accounts, then add the GOOGL and GOOG lines for each fund.

The holiday season has arrived, and with it, plenty of reasons your fitness routine may slide. Between shopping for gifts, attending holiday parties, and meeting work obligations, it can feel like there’s not enough time to squeeze in an hour-long workout session—so why even try?
Well, consider this: You don’t have to do as much as you think to maintain your fitness between now and New Year’s Day. A review published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021 suggests that you can reduce your workout time by two-thirds and still maintain your gains, as long as the intensity stays the same.
Researchers also found that, in generally active adults, cutting training frequency to just twice a week for up to 15 weeks could maintain short-term endurance and VO₂ max.
Setting an attainable goal for yourself, like running for at least 30 minutes two or three times per week, can make staying active through the holidays feel more doable. It’s how I was able to get back to exercise after a break, and it’s also how I plan to maintain my fitness this winter—in addition to following some of the best advice from my Runner’s World colleagues.
So ditch the all-or-nothing mindset and use the following tips to your advantage now, so when the New Year arrives, you’ll be ready to tackle your goals for 2027.
6 Tips for Maintaining Fitness During the Busy Holiday Season
1. Spice Up Your Usual Training Plan
“I have a race in mid-January, so I am following a training plan [which keeps me motivated]. But I am also cross-training with step aerobics, and I’ve added jump training into my workouts. I was bored with my usual strength routine, so I decided to mix things up with kettlebell training, targeting my upper body and core.” —Donna Raskin, senior health and fitness editor
“I make time for new workout classes, like the ones offered by Solidcore and OrangeTheory to support my strength needs, because I usually don’t get to attend those sessions when I’m training for a race.” —Sara Hemstock, senior director of marketing and brand liaison
“I love doing strength work and some form of speed training in the winter. I recently found an indoor track in my local YMCA, and I’m excited to use that as an option for when it snows. There’s something nostalgic about it for me after running winter track as a kid.” —Kristine Kearns, associate health and fitness editor
2. Turn a Run Into a Holiday Tradition
“I love running on Christmas Day because it’s always so quiet in my hometown of Columbia, South Carolina. I usually run downtown, past the state capitol building, and through the University of South Carolina. The normally busy area turns into a complete ghost town! It’s a once-a-year experience and a personal tradition. I look forward to it every year.” —Theo Khaler, news editor
3. Sign Up for a Local Race
“Every year, I look forward to going home to North Carolina during the holidays because I get to test my fitness in my neighborhood Turkey Trot. It’s a community event put on by my high school, and it always draws a huge crowd.
The 5K race itself gives me something to look toward and train for in the fall. It’s a great chance to test my speed and have fun with the sport, but the best part has to be the community aspect. I catch up with old friends, teammates, coaches, teachers, and neighbors, and hearing about their own running journeys always fuels mine, too. Plus, each age-group winner wins a pie. Who doesn’t like free dessert?” —Ashley Tysiac, content hype

Holding a stock through 2030 means keeping it for more than four years. A lot can go wrong with any one business in that time, so I'd rather not count on a single company for that long.
My three favorites today are Micron Technology (MU -2.52%), Amazon (AMZN -0.29%), and International Business Machines (IBM +1.00%). They don't look like much of a group. Micron stock trades at under 5 times the earnings analysts expect for this fiscal year, while Amazon trades at around 25 times earnings, using analysts' 2027 forecasts. And IBM's dividend yields about 2.8%.
But I think these differences are a big reason the three fit well together.
Image source: Micron.
1. Micron: The stock looks cheap for what it earns
Micron's growth in the last year has been stunning. Revenue more than tripled in fiscal 2026 to $133.2 billion (Micron's fiscal year ended Sept. 3, 2026), and net income climbed around tenfold to $85.0 billion.
The company's still growing, too. Revenue climbed to $54.2 billion in fiscal Q4 from $41.5 billion the quarter before, and management expects about $61.5 billion in the current one -- slower sequential growth, but growth all the same.
Yet at roughly $820 as of this writing, shares cost under 5 times earnings, using analysts' forecasts for fiscal 2027. In other words, investors are arguably pricing in a steep fall in profits at some point.
There's history behind this doubt. In fiscal 2023, Micron's revenue was around half the prior year's, and the company lost $5.8 billion.
MU Micron Technology
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/13/26
What makes me comfortable holding through 2030 is how much of the business is now under contract. Micron estimates that its 26 strategic customer agreements will make up over a third of its revenue through 2030. And most of that revenue comes with set pricing terms, often including floor and ceiling prices.
2. Amazon: AWS has years of work lined up
Amazon's cloud business is the top reason I'd hold the stock through 2030. Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue climbed 39% year over year to $46.0 billion in the third quarter, its fastest growth in almost five years. And AWS brought in about 63% of Amazon's operating income on about 23% of its sales.
What's more, AWS's backlog (contracted revenue it hasn't recognized yet) hit $578 billion. That's over three years of revenue at AWS's current $184 billion annual run rate.
"[W]e believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years," CEO Andy Jassy said on Amazon's third-quarter earnings call.

IBM is the slowest grower of the three. Management expects revenue to climb 4% to 5% at constant currency this year (a measure that removes exchange-rate changes).

His Credit Card May Cover a Broken or Stolen Phone, as Long as He Pays His Phone Bill With It
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A cracked screen or a stolen phone can lead to a costly repair or a new phone, but some cardholders already have coverage for this through a credit card. Credit card cell phone protection is a card benefit that can pay for a broken or stolen phone, as long as you pay your monthly wireless bill with that card.
A card benefit is a perk the issuer builds into the card at no separate charge, and a deductible is the amount the cardholder pays out of pocket on each claim before the benefit covers the rest.
How Paying the Phone Bill Switches On Coverage
Once the cardholder charges the monthly cell phone bill to an eligible card, the phones on that bill are covered against damage and theft. If something happens, the cardholder files a claim, pays the deductible, and gets reimbursed for a repair or replacement, and each card sets a limit per claim and a cap per year.
One Cellular Telephone Protection guide to benefits, as of 07/01/2021, spells out the schedule. Coverage starts the first day of the calendar month after a wireless bill is paid. If a month’s bill isn’t paid with the card, coverage is suspended until a later bill is paid with it.
What Two Big Issuers Publish Right Now
Limits vary from card to card. Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC | WFC Price Prediction) lists up to $600 of cell phone protection against damage or theft on its Active Cash card, subject to a $25 deductible. The product page compares benefits as of 04/28/2026, and the card has a $0 annual fee.
Capital One (NYSE:COF) says Venture X cardholders who pay their phone bill with the card can get reimbursed up to $800. The reimbursement applies if the phone is stolen or damaged. Terms, conditions, and exclusions apply. That card has a $395 annual fee.
The older guide lists lower limits than these two cards. It pays $200 per claim, with a maximum of two (2) claims and $400 per twelve (12) month period and a $50 deductible. Issuers update these benefits, so only the current guide for the specific card counts.
Which Phones Qualify and Which Get Left Out
Coverage generally follows the bill that was paid. Under the guide, eligible phones are the lines listed on the most recent wireless statement for the billing period before the event. A family plan paid with the card may cover every line on it. A phone on a separate bill paid some other way doesn’t qualify.
The same guide also excludes rented and borrowed phones, phones on pre-paid or “pay as you go” plans, and phones bought for resale or commercial use.
Requirements for Keeping Coverage Active Before the Next Drop
- The card’s Guide to Benefits lists the terms. Wells Fargo tells cardholders to call the number on the back of the card to request a copy.
- The guide lists the per-claim limit, the yearly cap, the deductible, and the claim deadlines.
- Coverage requires the monthly wireless bill to be paid with that card.
- Copies of wireless statements show the card payment.
- After a theft, the guide requires a police report, filed within forty-eight (48) hours.
- Claims usually rely on repair estimates, receipts, and photos of the damage.
Exclusions That Can Block a Claim
Lost phones are a common gap. The guide excludes phones that are lost or “mysteriously disappear” with no evidence that someone took them.

"This is actually a bigger deal for humanity than most people can imagine," Walter Isaacson, Elon Musk's biographer, wrote on X after SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) caught its Starship spacecraft with the launch tower's arms on Nov. 14. Musk shared the post with a message of his own: "The epic day has arrived, thanks to the incredibly talented team at SpaceX!"
Isaacson also recalled the engineers' reactions in a Starbase conference room in December 2020, when Musk pushed the idea that the tower's arms could catch a returning Starship.
Hours after the catch, Musk reshared his Aug. 30, 2021, post calling the tower arms "robot chopsticks," which warned that "success is not guaranteed, but excitement is!" On Flight 15, he got half of each. The rocket's Super Heavy booster, which was supposed to be caught the same way, was diverted and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX has caught three earlier versions of the booster, the first in October 2024, but this was the first attempt with its newest design.
SpaceX shares closed at $139.11 on Nov. 13, about 3% above the $135 IPO price, then slipped about 2% in after-hours trading as the booster was lost. Nov. 16 is the market's first chance to react to the catch. The next test comes Dec. 8, when the last batch of insider shares from the IPO lockup can be sold.
Ship 42 kept climbing into orbit, which Starship first reached on the previous flight, on Sept. 28. About 35 minutes after liftoff, it began releasing 26 Starlink V3 satellites, a batch SpaceX says adds roughly 10 times the downlink capacity of a Falcon 9 Starlink launch. Three of the satellites carried cameras to photograph the ship's heat shield, which SpaceX checked before committing to bring it home. The ship then circled Earth about 14 times.
Musk and SpaceX engineers were inspecting the ship within hours. "I hugged ship 42 upon its return," he posted, along with videos showing it "looks great!"
The ship's condition matters because SpaceX wants to fly it again. A reusable rocket is supposed to make launches far cheaper, and cheaper launches mean more Starlink satellites. SpaceX told CNN it aims to reliably reuse Starship by NASA's Artemis IV moon mission, slated for 2028, though NASA hasn't decided whether Starship or Blue Origin's Blue Moon will land that crew.
Before the flight, Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas called a successful catch one of the most significant potential catalysts in SpaceX's history.
You may think you own a rocket company
In the third quarter, SpaceX reported revenue of $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year earlier and well above the $12.72 billion analysts expected. Net income was $4.4 billion, helped by about $1 billion of other income and a $390 million tax benefit. Income from operations was $2.8 billion.
Its AI business, which the company calls "Super Intelligence," brought in $7.56 billion, topping the $5.25 billion from Connectivity, the segment that includes Starlink, for the first time. The Space segment, home to Starship, lost $7 million as research spending on the rocket rose.
Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers at Sept. 30. Average monthly revenue per user rose to $69 from $66 in the second quarter but was still below $83 a year earlier. SpaceX is also pushing Starlink into the phone business.
Cheap launches matter to the stock because SpaceX is its own biggest customer. Of the 476 metric tons it put in orbit last quarter, 358 were its own payloads.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2025 issue of Runner’s World.
“What fresh hell is this?” Liz B. wondered during a four-mile run on a chilly December night five months after giving birth. She was 2.7 miles into an out-and-back route when she realized she’d leaked a little urine. “It happened on and off the rest of the way home,” says the 36-year-old from central Ohio, who prefers not to use her full name when talking about urinary incontinence, which affects 25 million adult Americans.
This was not how she had envisioned her postpartum life. Liz, a physical therapist who works with stroke, brain injury, and spinal cord injury patients, had been a runner for nearly her whole life. Her father, who just ran his 91st marathon at the age of 77, had taken her out for jogs when she was a toddler, and she was hooked on long distances ever since. Her idea of a “good time” was waking up at 5 a.m. on a Saturday to go for a scenic 16-mile run with her sister. Before becoming a mom, she’d run eight marathons and was eight minutes shy of qualifying for Boston. “I had always been excited to get pregnant and had dreams of pushing my kid in a running stroller.” But her regular runs came to a screeching halt 19 weeks into her pregnancy when she developed peripheral blood clots and had to reduce physical activity because of the pain. She’d been looking forward to lacing up her running shoes again, but after a difficult labor, she developed pelvic organ prolapse, a condition where weak muscles allow one or more pelvic organs (like the uterus or bladder) to drop down onto other organs or out of the vagina.
Liz had been working with a pelvic floor therapist to treat the prolapse and had just spent the previous six weeks easing back into running. But she was frustrated with the slow progress in coming back to her pre-pregnancy eight-minute mile. “Once I had my baby, my pace slowed to a 10:30 mile,” Liz says. “And if I ran under a 9:00, I’d pee my pants a little.”
Pelvic floor dysfunction, an inability to coordinate pelvic floor muscles, is more prevalent than most of us realize. Research shows that approximately 1 in 3 women and 1 in 6 men will experience pelvic floor dysfunction in their lifetime—and that’s just what gets reported. Particularly in women, hormonal fluctuations, added weight, and the strain of pregnancy and childbirth can weaken the pelvic floor.
As much as we dislike the fact, high-impact physical activity—like running—can exacerbate these issues. That’s because as you run, your pelvic floor repeatedly absorbs impact and dampens vibrations, says Julie W. Wiebe, DPT, a physical therapist in Los Angeles who specializes in returning women to fitness after injury and pregnancy.
“Running creates an added challenge to your pelvic floor beyond the movements of everyday activities,” explains Carrie Pagliano, PT, a pelvic floor specialist based in Arlington, Virginia. “It puts greater impact and pressure on your musculoskeletal system.”
The good news is these issues can be resolved. But too often, they go undiagnosed. For one thing, there’s the stigma. Talking about pelvic floor issues can feel taboo because we’ve been conditioned to have shame around that area of the body. What’s more, most of us aren’t even sure where our pelvic floor is, what it does, or how it can become dysfunctional.
